answer:
So I had a chance to interview two great CIOs recently, both doing incredible things with their companies:
Mark Hurd, former President and COO of Oracle, now leading the charge at Workday
Jim Goldenberg, former Chief Information Officer at DISH Network, where he oversaw IT infrastructure across North America
Both were part of our SaaStr Annual speaker line-up this year and did deep dives with me on how they buy software — especially Cloud-based solutions. And what really came through was that while both come from “big tech” backgrounds, today they work in environments where they need help. Where there aren’t enough resources to get everything done. Jim described his team at Dish as like a tiny army. He has just one security engineer to protect Dish’s entire network! Both shared something interesting. Mark Hurd noted he works hard every day because no matter how well you build your team, someone else can always take advantage of you. Jim said he also spends a lot of time helping people learn new skills, and trying to find other ways to leverage limited resources. That doesn’t mean either isn’t incredibly successful in scaling massive organizations. But it does show that even folks running multi-billion dollar businesses still have to hustle when times are tough. So why would anyone want to buy software from a tiny start-up? Especially if it might be less reliable than Big Tech’s product? A few thoughts here:
First, some CIOs may not care so much if the solution is stable or not. They’re already over budget anyway, and often under-staffed. Maybe they’d prefer to spend money on multiple vendors, if each vendor could deliver incremental value. Second, many CIOs don’t see the point in buying enterprise-grade functionality until the company is ready for it.

I've been doing this now for over 20 years. I've done some big deals, but mostly I've done lots and lots of little ones. So today's topic is how does a tiny start-up, maybe even one that doesn't have enough revenue to support two sales reps yet, go into the enterprise and win a deal with like a Fortune 500 company or something bigger than that?
And my take is it can be done. It has to happen again and again and again. And we're going to talk about what the social contract is between a buyer and seller here because if you understand the social contract and you deliver value within the constraints of the social contract, then you will get funded by the customer. They'll buy more stuff from you. There's nothing magic here, but there are rules. Let me tell you when I first started in tech, I worked at Adobe Sign, which is also known as EchoSign back in the day. We were five people, six people, eight people. We had no real brand name. But we won our first Fortune 1000 deal after three months with just five people on the team. We did it against Salesforce, Atlassian, Marketo, and another vendor. That was tough.
But the reason they picked us was because we showed up. We actually showed up. We didn't send someone who said he would follow up later. We sent people who knew everything about the product cold and could demo it live. They trusted us. So trust is key, but let's break down the other parts too because there's always the elephant in the room when you're talking about a lot of money.

Hey everyone,
I'm excited today to dig into an interesting case study we've never done before on SaaStr. We're gonna go back in time a few years to look at Monday dot com's first public filing at $250 million in ARR. You might wonder why? Well, there were two reasons really. First, it was my first SaaS investment ever. It's a big milestone for me and one I'll always remember. Second, what happened after their first public filing at $250M in ARR is something most of us will never experience. They went from $300M to almost $600M in ARR in less than three years. A truly epic run. So let's take a quick look back, and then fast forward to where they are today at $540m in ARR.
So Monday is probably the last of our "classic" SaaS companies to file to IPO. Many of them, from PagerDuty to Slack to Snowflake, have already gone public. But Monday held off until it got past $100m in ARR, and when it did, boy oh boy, it grew like crazy. Let's take a look at what happened between that initial public filing at $250m ARR, and their second one later at $450m in ARR. Just wow. Incredibly impressive growth.
A few interesting learnings:

First, while Monday started off with very small businesses, by the time they filed for their second IPO at $450m in ARR, bigger customers had become 60% of their base. Today, Monday says 70% of its customers pay $50k or more annually. Wow. What a change over just 3-4 years!  This is a great example of the power of going up-market in SaaS. Even though it wasn’t always clear to me how much they’d do it, I think Monday’s decision to focus more on mid-sized and enterprise customers post-IPO is one reason they’ve been able to grow so rapidly since then.
Second, at $350m in ARR, Monday said 78% of its customer count came from its top 20 customers. Now this isn’t unusual per se — often times, the largest customers end up being 30%-40% of the revenue, even if they aren’t 30%-40% of the customer count. But at $350m, Monday’s Top 20 customers made up 80% of their revenues.
